      <h1>Central AI Team Charter — Mandate, First Loop, and the Reuse Metric</h1>
      <p class="ws-sub">A signed central AI team charter with a named first loop and a reuse-based success metric — the staffing decision the chapter calls among the highest-leverage in the program.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="ws-meta">
      <b>WS-07-central-team-charter</b><br>

    <a href="https://danielmeppiel.github.io/agentic-sdlc-handbook/handbook/ch07-the-agentic-sdlc-bill.html#sec-bill-staff-the-factory">#sec-bill-staff-the-factory</a>
    &middot; Locator: “The roles already exist in this book. The Agentic Workflow Engineer”
  </div>

  <div class="ws-instruction">
    Complete the left page first: record which working patterns you have and which anti-patterns you refuse, with evidence and mechanisms. Then charter the team, its first recurring ROI-positive loop, its distribution path and its mandatory reuse metric; set the escape hatch and assign all six lifecycle stages. On the last sheet, answer whether this charter is the anti-pattern and write three mechanism-backed commitments. Have the accountable executive and the person who would become the bottleneck sign.
  </div>

          </colgroup>
          <thead>

          </thead>
          <tbody>

              <td><b>Working pattern</b></td>
              <td class="prior">Stream-aligned teams with embedded context engineering / a platform team providing shared context infrastructure / a time-boxed enabling team for adoption support<span class="prior-src">ch06 L228-232</span></td>
              <td class="locked">Fixed pattern list; record status in field 3.</td>

              <td class="locked">Printed reasoning; read-only.</td>

      <div class="ws-block">
        <h2>Block B — the three shapes we refuse to build
          <span class="ws-block-note">status, evidence and mechanism for each</span></h2>
        <table class="ws">
          <colgroup>
            <col style="width:6%"><col style="width:20%"><col style="width:36%"><col style="width:38%">
          </colgroup>
          <thead>
            <tr><th></th><th>Field</th><th>What the book says</th><th>Your answer</th></tr>
          </thead>
          <tbody>
            <tr>
              <td class="ws-num"><span class="fno">6</span></td>
              <td><b>Anti-pattern</b></td>
              <td class="prior">A centralised “AI team” that handles all agent interactions / splitting “human code” and “agent code” into separate workflows / replacing team roles with agents<span class="prior-src">ch06 L236-240</span></td>
              <td class="locked">Fixed anti-pattern list; record status in field 8.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td class="ws-num"><span class="fno">7</span></td>
              <td><b>Why the chapter says it fails</b></td>
              <td class="prior">
                Row 1: a specialised group becomes <b>the bottleneck for all agent work</b>; the result is a coordination tax that eliminates the speed advantage, and a knowledge gap because the AI team does not understand each product domain deeply enough to write good context.<br>
                Row 2: some organizations try to create parallel tracks: human engineers handle “important” code, agents handle “routine” code. This fails because the boundary between important and routine is not stable, agent code still requires human review and integration, and a two-class system undermines cohesion — all code is the team’s code regardless of who or what produced it.<br>
                Row 3: teams that lose senior engineers because “the AI can do that now” lose the judgement required to evaluate agent output and maintain architectural coherence, and produce more code and less working software.
                <span class="prior-src">ch06 L236-240</span>
              </td>
              <td class="locked">Printed reasoning; read-only.</td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td class="ws-num"><span class="fno">8</span></td>
              <td><b>Status here</b></td>
              <td class="prior">—<span class="prior-src">org</span></td>

                <b>Centralised AI team as the funnel</b><div class="f-select"><span class="opt">not present</span><span class="opt">at risk</span><span class="opt">already happening</span></div>
                <b>Separate human-code / agent-code tracks</b><div class="f-select"><span class="opt">not present</span><span class="opt">at risk</span><span class="opt">already happening</span></div>
                <b>Replacing team roles with agents</b><div class="f-select"><span class="opt">not present</span><span class="opt">at risk</span><span class="opt">already happening</span></div>
              </td>

                <b>Separate human-code / agent-code tracks</b><span class="f-text"></span>
                <b>Replacing team roles with agents</b><span class="f-text"></span>
                <span class="ours-label">What you observed. “We would never do that” is not evidence.</span>
              </td>
            </tr>
            <tr>
              <td class="ws-num"><span class="fno">10</span></td>
              <td><b>What specifically prevents it</b></td>
              <td class="prior">—<span class="prior-src">derived</span></td>

                <b>Centralised AI team as the funnel</b><span class="f-text"></span>

                <b>Replacing team roles with agents</b><span class="f-text"></span>
              </td>
            </tr>
